title: Build a Command-Line Calculator
learningObjectives: Describe the purpose and scope of build a command-line calculator.
Plan the required data, inputs, outputs, and behaviors.
Break the solution into manageable functions or steps.
Implement and test normal, invalid, and boundary cases.
Review the result and explain limitations and improvements.

understand.concept: A command-line calculator accepts operands and an operation, validates the input, computes a result, and presents it clearly. The project should separate parsing, validation, calculation, and display so errors are handled deliberately. A calculator is small enough to test thoroughly but contains many core programming concepts.
understand.whyItMatters: This project turns variables, input/output, conditions, functions, validation, and tests into a complete working program.
understand.analogy: Think of completing a small real-world task by defining the goal, organizing the work, checking each step, and reviewing the finished result.
understand.analogyLimit: Software projects require precise requirements, data and code design, technical testing, and iterative change; the analogy only introduces a workflow.

explain.narrative:
A command-line calculator accepts operands and an operation, validates the input, computes a result, and presents it clearly. The project should separate parsing, validation, calculation, and display so errors are handled deliberately. A calculator is small enough to test thoroughly but contains many core programming concepts.

Build incrementally and keep the project scope appropriate for your current skills. The examples illustrate individual design steps; they are not a complete ready-made project. Test your own implementation and document assumptions.

examples.title: Define supported operations
examples.explanation: A clear operation list defines the first scope.

examples.title: Calculate addition
examples.explanation: Calculation is isolated in a function.

examples.title: Guard division by zero
examples.code:
function divide(a,b){if(b===0)return 'cannot divide by zero';return a/b;}
console.log(divide(9,0));
examples.explanation: Invalid math cases are handled explicitly.

commonMistakes: Starting implementation without defining scope or acceptance criteria.
Combining input, logic, and display in one tangled block.
Claiming features or data persist when they are only in memory.
Adding features before the core workflow works and is tested.

guidedTask.title: Guided Project
guidedTask.instructions: Build a calculator that supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Start with a menu or operation prompt. Parse inputs, validate them, call a calculation function, display the result, and handle division by zero.
steps: Build a calculator that supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Start with a menu or operation prompt. Parse inputs, validate them, call a calculation function, display the result, and handle division by zero.
Write a short scope and acceptance checklist.
Test a normal case and at least two edge/error cases.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Project starter: define requirements and functions before writing the complete program.

independentTask.title: Independent Project
independentTask.instructions: Extend the calculator with a loop, clear exit option, repeated calculations, decimal inputs, invalid operation handling, and a test table covering normal and edge cases.
requirements: Keep the project original and appropriately scoped.
Extend the calculator with a loop, clear exit option, repeated calculations, decimal inputs, invalid operation handling, and a test table covering normal and edge cases.
Include a short test plan and results.

hints: Keep calculation functions separate from input handling.
Convert inputs deliberately and check conversion success.
Treat division by zero as a special case.
Use a loop only if you can clearly exit it.
Test positive, negative, decimal, and invalid values.
